content:
The stage play "We Are the Happiest" (《我們最快樂》), which had its performance cancelled by the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, has been brought to Japan by Mount Zao Bookstore (見山書店). Yesterday (the 16th), at the Home/Work Village in Setagaya Ward, Tokyo, Japanese actors read out the translated script, and a creative symposium was also held. The playwright Alice Chong (莊梅岩) and actor Anthony Wong (黃秋生) both attended to share their insights, attracting over a hundred Hong Kong and Japanese audience members. At the sharing session, when Alice Chong was asked about the impact of being unable to stage the work in Hong Kong, she admitted that her emotions fluctuated greatly, and sometimes she felt very down, but said that the experience of being blacklisted gave her "valuable experience," which Anthony Wong described as "immersive learning." Alice Chong said the description was apt, and noted that "the blows you don't see are even more numerous." Anthony Wong responded with "I feel the same way." Alice Chong said she hopes that one day she can write about "all the various blows that you cannot understand today."

Mount Zao Bookstore has opened a limited-time bookstore called "Summer Vacation in a Foreign Country" (異國嘅暑假) at the Home/Work Village in Setagaya Ward, with activities including a two-day reading of "We Are the Happiest."

Enthusiastic audience response, additional performances added

This performance was a key activity of "Summer Vacation in a Foreign Country (異国の夏休み)," a limited-time bookstore opened in Tokyo between July and September by the now-suspended independent bookstore "Mount Zao Bookstore." It also marks the latest work by Alice Chong to be performed in Japan, following earlier productions including "Liu Shou Tai Ping Jian" (《留守太平間》), "May 35" (《五月三十五》) and "Wild Boar" (《野豬》).

Mount Zao Bookstore manager Sharon described the impetus for this performance as a "telepathy" (心有靈犀) with Alice Chong, as both hoped to bring good things to Japan to share, leading to this reading and symposium. Sharon had been worried about ticket sales, so she did not dare to book too large a venue, but the first session's over one hundred tickets sold out within two days. Ultimately, she decided to add a performance at the gymnasium within Home/Work Village, and those tickets also sold out completely within a few days.

Mount Zao Bookstore manager Sharon said that the "telepathy" with Alice Chong in hoping to bring good things to Japan to share led to this reading and symposium.

Translated script read by Japanese actors, Anthony Wong: emotion has nothing to do with language

"We Are the Happiest" tells the story of a young gay male couple — articled clerk Philip and Ah Sang (阿生) — whose relationship undergoes changes and heads towards a tragic结局 after the intervention of Philip's boss Neil. The play had its premiere in 2022 and was originally scheduled for a re-run late last year, but the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority said it had received complaints that the play "promoted confrontation and denigrated Hong Kong," and cancelled the venue and performance.

For this performance, Hong Kong-based director in Japan Indi Chan condensed the original approximately two-hour performance into one hour, and had three Japanese actors — Egami Shingo (江上真悟) as Neil, Nakanishi Ryosuke (中西良介) as Philip, and Kikuchi Kanki (菊地かんき) as Ah Sang — perform the translated Japanese text in a reading format. After the reading, a creative sharing session was held with playwright Alice Chong and Anthony Wong, who was originally cast as Neil in the play, along with the director and actors.

Three Japanese actors performed the translated Japanese text in a reading format.

Among the ticketed audience, approximately one-third were from Hong Kong, with the rest being Japanese audience members. While watching the performance, many audience members opened either the Chinese or Japanese script collections and followed along with the actors' reading, Anthony Wong being one of them. During the sharing session, he recalled that his teacher during his time at the Academy of Performing Arts had taught him that "emotion has nothing to do with language," and said he was surprised that despite not understanding Japanese, he was able to follow the progress of the performance during his first time reading a Chinese script alongside a foreign-language performance, and highly praised the outstanding performance of the three Japanese actors.

During the performance, many audience members, including Anthony Wong, opened either the Chinese or Japanese script collections and followed along with the actors' reading. He was surprised that despite not understanding Japanese, he was able to follow the progress of the performance, recalling that his teacher had once taught him that "emotion has nothing to do with language."

Anthony Wong also expressed hope that "We Are the Happiest" could have a full performance in Japan, joking that he would have to learn Japanese in order to play the youthful characters in the play. In addition to the symposium, he also welcomed collaboration with figures from the Japanese art world in areas such as performance. This time, he also brought eight paintings to participate in "Summer Vacation in a Foreign Country," hoping to hold a solo painting exhibition in Japan next year.

Anthony Wong this time also brought eight paintings imitating Matisse to participate in "Summer Vacation in a Foreign Country," hoping to hold a solo painting exhibition in Japan next year.

Alice Chong: gained experience from being blacklisted; Anthony Wong: immersive learning

When asked about the impact on her creative work of being unable to stage the piece in Hong Kong, Alice Chong responded that public performances allow her to review the presentation of her text, constituting "the final step in a playwright's learning process during creation." The inability to stage a production dealt a heavy blow to her, who loves the stage, saying "My emotions fluctuate greatly; I'm relatively happier now that I'm in Japan, but sometimes I feel very down." As for how she creates under such circumstances, she said she is still "adapting," but that even without being able to perform, she can continue to write, and is still creating works.

Alice Chong drew on her reading of "Things in nature merely grow," sharing a resonance with the author whose two sons died by suicide, emphasizing that the experience of being blacklisted gave her "a different feeling of understanding what others go through," and yielded "valuable experience." Anthony Wong said this was "immersive learning," drawing laughter from the audience. Alice Chong also laughed and said the description was apt, because "the blows you see are only the blows you see; for me, in every aspect, the blows you don't see are even more numerous." Anthony Wong responded, "I deeply empathize with your misfortune." Alice Chong stated directly, "All the various blows that you cannot understand today, there will come a day when I hope I can write them out," and said she would write them together with Anthony Wong's share.

After the reading ended, playwright Alice Chong and Anthony Wong, who was originally cast as Neil in the play, held a creative sharing session with the director and actors.

Alice Chong points to regression in the situation for homosexuals; Anthony Wong uses the cha-cha as an analogy

Nakanishi Ryosuke, who played Philip, said that performing in "We Are the Happiest" reminded him of the Japanese literary work "The Tale of Genji," written over a thousand years ago, in which characters, unable to attain love, would kill or kill themselves. He had previously had doubts about such depictions, but found that a thousand years later, this script from Hong Kong contained the same plot elements, so he said he "began to understand a little of this state of mind." Alice Chong explained that although the protagonists are homosexuals, the exploration of obsession with love and desire in the story transcends sexual orientation and national boundaries.

In response to the different performance location, Indi made changes to the original final scene, and added legislation related to homosexuals in Hong Kong and Japan as background. At the sharing session, Indi mentioned that "whether in Hong Kong or Japan, same-sex couples are still unable to marry under the law," and called on the audience to continue paying attention to their rights. Alice Chong said that in the area of homosexuality, she felt that Hong Kong and other places had "actually regressed in many ways," and she did not dare to say that the next generation would be more open. Anthony Wong used the cha-cha as an analogy, saying that "the laws of social development are not a straight line," and that moving forward and backward is the norm.

An audience member wearing a "We Are the Happiest" commemorative T-shirt asked questions of Anthony Wong and Alice Chong.

Audience: as long as it's a good work, there will be people who appreciate it

Japanese audience Ms. Nakamura Miona (中村萌那), who had purchased tickets for the originally scheduled West Kowloon performance, said after participating in the event that she was "very happy to be able to see the Japanese actors' interpretation in Tokyo, but it also brought back the feeling of not being able to see the performance in Hong Kong at that time." She said she was curious about how Anthony Wong would portray the character of Neil, and looked forward to having the opportunity to see a full stage performance in Japan.

Hong Kong audience Ms. So (蘇小姐) had also purchased tickets for "We Are the Happiest," and specifically extended her stay in Japan in order to attend this symposium. Ms. So believed that this performance was an example of how there are still many people seeking out different spaces to demonstrate their power, saying "as long as it's a good work, there will be people who appreciate it, and no matter where or in what form, it can move other people."

Japanese audience Ms. Nakamura Miona, who had purchased tickets for the originally scheduled West Kowloon performance, said she was very happy to be able to see the Japanese actors' interpretation in Tokyo.
